english: Why does your family's herd lie in the fields? Sickness seized it. Three cows died yesterday. What will you do? I will burn the dead ones in fire. Drive your own herd away. I will drive it far. The immortals protect us.
uncertain: h₂éǵrōs acc. pl. with légʰeti (expected locative)
n̥ḱéwih₂n̥s read as 'dead ones' (fem. acc. pl.)
reviewer seen the whole packet PIE only, no English

english: The shepherd had a hundred sheep. Sickness came upon them in one winter. They coughed and grew weak and could not stand. The shepherd burned the dead ones in a great fire. Ten sheep remained. He drove them far away. In summer they were healthy/lambing. The shepherd praised the immortals.

In one summer it did not rain. The river dried up and the grain was dry. The cattle stood at the riverbank(?) and saw no water. The king led the clans to the sacred place. They took counsel: 'To Perkunos we will give the greatest ox.' They slew the ox on a stone and smoke went up to the sky. Then Perkunos thundered and it rained. The mortals rejoiced.

Did you find the beast in the hills? I found nothing. The wolves devoured the beasts. Are the wolves still hungry? They are hungry. They came into the enclosure at night. Now protect the young ones. I fear the wolves. I will guard them with dogs.
uncertain: ǵʰwḗrm̥ singular vs plural in answer

english: Father, the ground is frozen. How shall we bury her? Let us lay your mother in the snow and cover her with stones. The wolves will find her. They will not find her; the stones are great. When summer comes, let us lay her in the earth. Now let us sing her praise.

Son, the sickness carried me off this night. What are you saying? I, (for) the old and the grandchildren, devoured my food. I do not leave you in sickness. Hunger seized the grandchildren. May the sickness seize me and not seize them. I weep, and I carry you.
uncertain: third sentence unclear: gʷr̥h₃óh₂ 'I devour' with ǵérh₂onts acc. pl. and n̥ptṓm gen. pl. makes little sense
